patch.title: AI emulators of space physics codes with stated error bounds
patch.description: The weather-model playbook - train on decades of simulation or reanalysis data, run ~1,000x cheaper - applied to space codes (CFD and aerothermal, plasma, thermosphere, structures), with calibrated uncertainty or error bounds relative to the parent code; using them for margins still requires validation against test or flight data.
patch.why: Emulators remove the compute cost of design loops and ensembles. Weather moved from research models to operations in about 15 months on the back of 40+ years of reanalysis. Space domains split: where training data can be generated by simulation (CFD, structures, thermal) emulators are data-unconstrained and arrive first; where data come only from nature (one Sun, rare extreme storms, few hypersonic flights) they arrive late and extrapolate poorly. AIFS and Surya were built without research-grade applied math, so AI applied math accelerates this node (code-relative error bounds) rather than gating it; any certificate bounds error against the code, not against physics. Pathway P4 (a faster method with practical constants entering codes); band above the P4 default because the AIFS precedent shows research-to-operations inside ~15 months.

Environmental caps also bind: Starbase 25 a year (FAA, May 2025), LC-39A 44 (Jan 2026) and SLC-37 76 (Dec 2025), so 100 flights needs both Florida sites running above half their caps. Chain (S2): first V3 reflights 2027 -> four pads with pipeline or on-site propellant 2029 -> 100+ flights 2030; S3 2029 only if the four-pad set is ready early that year; S1 about 2030 on SpaceX's own trajectory. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here).

patch.title: AI cuts development cost of new space hardware by about 10-20%
patch.description: Non-recurring development cost for new spacecraft and launch vehicles falls about 10-20% under S2 as engineering labor for analysis, design, software and verification shrinks; hardware, test articles and facilities do not shrink.
patch.status_oct2026: Starship program spend exceeded $15B by 2026, against roughly $400M for Falcon 9 development, and SpaceX directed all $3B of its 2025 space-segment R&D to Starship (Reuters via 33FG). SpaceX held $100.8B in cash after an $85.7B IPO in June 2026.
patch.why: If engineering labor is 40-60% of development cost and analysis, design, software and verification are about half of it (general), S2's 5-10x cognitive speedup removes roughly 16-27% of total cost gross (merely halving that content removes 10-15%). physclock.json's capital row gives a 15-30% fall in development labor cost, which is about 6-18% of total cost, and an effective capital multiplier of 1.15-1.3x (13-23%). Scope growth takes some back, so the realized cut is about 10-20%. A second channel could add to it: standing-army costs scale with schedule, so shorter programs also trim time-proportional overhead. Chain (S2): engineering adoption 2028 -> programs started 2028 or later estimated with AI-reduced labor -> first program estimates showing 10-20% lower non-recurring cost 2029 -> completed-program evidence 2031 or later. S3: adoption 2028 with near-free cognition from 2029 -> 2029. S1: 2031. It matters most for capital-gated new entrants; for SpaceX capital is not binding through 2031. What binds is organizations changing practice, not capital.
patch.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): Skeptic: headline 15-30% did not follow from its own derivation (a labor figure presented as total cost), now about 10-20%; S3 2028 -> 2029; gate capital -> adoption. Auditor: chain written out; off-topic orbital-compute line removed. Advocate: soft edges from cost-collapse and program-cycle-compression and the standing-army channel added; advocate's S2 High rejected (by 2031 the evidence is mostly estimates and scope growth is the node's own strongest case).

patch.status_oct2026: Starlink: v0.9 May 2019, v1.0 late 2019, v1.5 2021, v2 mini Feb 2023, v2 mini optimized (average satellite mass down from 623 kg to 575 kg, 96 Gbps), V3 (about 1 Tbps, about 2 t) first flown on Flight 13 (Jul 2026) and first orbited on Flight 14 (Sep 28 2026). V3's timing was gated by Starship, not the satellite. V2 mini production reached six a day by Mar 2023 (Wikipedia; Mach33). SpaceX's first compute satellite, Starmind AI1 (spec disclosed Jun 2026), uses modular, interchangeable chip inserts, and its power target rose from 150 kW (Jun) to about 250 kW (Oct 2026) (Mach33).
patch.why: Chain (S2): engineering adoption 2028 -> first AI-era bus or payload designed, qualified and retooled in about 12-15 months -> fielded 2029 -> a second generation about 12 months later shows the cadence, 2030. S3: same adoption year, but commercial generations compress 0.5-0.7x (18-36 months becomes 9-25), so 2029 at the optimistic edge; an annual cadence sits at the favorable end even there, so Medium. Design, software and verification compress in S2; payload qualification, radiation testing, line retooling and the launcher bind (V3's timing was set by Starship). Upside not driven by AI math: orbital-compute satellites may track the accelerator makers' annual cadence (general) with modular chip inserts on a common bus, making a yearly payload generation a chip swap. Faster generations raise capacity per kilogram (V3 carries about three times V2 mini's capacity per kilogram, Mach33).

Advocate: optimal-test-campaigns hard -> soft (Starlink iterated without them), soft edge from starship-full-reuse, AI1 modular-insert status added; advocate's S2 High rejected (the chip-cadence mechanism is not AI-math-driven and depends on unproven orbital-compute economics).

patch.title: Development cycles shrink by a quarter to a third, not 10x
patch.description: Development time (concept to launch) for new space systems started after AI adoption falls measurably. Amdahl ceiling: about 38% shorter in S2 (51% in S3, 18% in S1) if a third of the critical path is cognitive and fully compressible. Expected realized compression for typical programs started in 2028 or later: about 20-30% in S2 (about 35-45% in S3, 10-15% in S1), with fast commercial programs nearer the ceiling and government flagships at 10-15% (appropriations).
patch.why: Illustrative critical-path shares (general): requirements and trades 10%, design and analysis 15%, software 10%, fabrication and procurement 25%, integration and test 25%, qualification and reviews 10%, launch campaign 5%. Speedups of 5-10x on cognitive work and 1.1-1.2x on physical work (S2) give a 1.6x speedup, a ~38% shorter schedule; S3 (20-50x cognitive, 1.3-1.5x physical) ~51%; S1 (2x cognitive) ~18%. These are ceilings: they assume every cognitive step is on the critical path and fully compressible. Requirements negotiation, hardware-in-the-loop software testing and review gates compress far less, and long-lead parts (12-24+ months) often run in parallel with design, so compressing design can leave the critical path unchanged; each 10 points of effectively compressible cognitive share is worth about 7 points of compression. Counting more of the analysis inside test and build phases as cognitive (anomaly diagnosis, procedures, data reduction, material-review paperwork) lifts the S2 ceiling to roughly 45%, but the table's 1.1-1.2x physical multipliers already credit about 10 of those 60 points (if the residual physical work runs at 1.0x), so most of that gain is already inside the 38%. Fewer design escapes found in test cut rework, a second-order gain. Chain (S2): engineering adoption 2028 -> commercial programs started 2028 or later (smallsat lag ladder 12-18 months) -> first completions 2029-30 -> an attributable schedule analysis 2031. S3: 2030. Band Medium: evidence must come from programs started after adoption and finished by 2031, and government flagships dilute any average. Uncrewed commercial programs need no certifier, so the binding gate is integration and test hardware (experiment), not qualification.
patch.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): Debated (skeptic vs advocate, auditor on wording). Skeptic accepted: 38% is a ceiling, realized lower; S2 2030 -> 2031, S3 2029 -> 2030 (only post-adoption programs count). Advocate partly accepted: the qualification cap was misapplied (gate -> experiment), cap-design-optimization hard -> soft, soft edges from mishap analysis and cheap mass; its 35-50% S2 figure rejected as largely double-counting what the 1.1-1.2x physical multipliers already credit, and its S2 2029 / S3 High rejected (depended on adoption in 2027). Realized range set at 20-30% in S2 between the skeptic's 15-25% and the advocate's 35-50%.

patch.description: Third-party customers can routinely buy dedicated heavy-lift launch below $1,000 per kilogram of customer payload delivered (not per kilogram of vehicle capacity), against a Falcon 9 dedicated median of about $5,300/kg and a rideshare floor of about $7,000/kg today.

AI math reaches this node only by speeding competitors' engineering. Mach33's 2035 simulations vary when SpaceX releases Starship's spare capacity to customers (2029-2033) as a main price driver, so competition accelerates this node rather than gating it, and SpaceX can price below $1,000/kg without a rival; internal orbital-compute demand can delay that release. Band S2 Low: Mach33's fade midpoint is 2033 (range 2030-36), so crossing by 2031 is roughly 20-30% (judgment), and AI moves it 0-1 year. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here).

patch.description: A program in any country started in 2027 or later reaches orbit with a reusable medium or heavy launcher within three years of program start.
patch.why: Even with cognitive work nearly free, engine development (hot-fire campaigns, turbopump failures), pad construction (2-4 years) and flight-test learning set a floor of about 4-5 years. AI's best case removes about a year, and only programs started after AI adoption (2027-28 in S2) benefit. The realistic path is a derivative built around an existing engine family: LandSpace's Zhuque-3 (TQ-12-family methalox engines from Zhuque-2) hopped in Jan 2024, reached orbit Dec 3 2025 and landed its first stage on its second flight, Aug 18 2026 (Wikipedia), on roughly a four-year derivative timeline without AI help (general). Clean-sheet multipliers of 0.8-0.9x (S2) and 0.7-0.8x (S3) on such a timeline give about 3.2-3.6 years in S2, so Speculative, and 2.8-3.2 years in S3, so Low. FAA licensing reform and AI-run test stands help U.S. entrants but are not gates for every entrant.

add_nodes.title: AI compute becomes Starship's second anchor customer
add_nodes.description: Orbital-compute satellites (SpaceX Starmind AI1 and peers) fill at least 10 Starship flights in one calendar year, so Starship cadence and production learning depend on AI compute demand as well as Starlink. This couples the launch clock to the AI capability curve through demand, not through mathematics.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Not yet. SpaceX disclosed AI1's first specification in Jun 2026 (150 kW peak compute; about 2.1 t implied by Mach33's reconstruction, with modular, interchangeable chip inserts) and partnered with Nvidia on its compute payload (Rubin GPUs and Vera CPUs; SpaceX, Aug 4 2026, via 33FG). Mach33 reports the power target rising to about 250 kW by Oct 2026 and calls space datacenters the largest uncertainty in its Starship launch-revenue model (Sep 2026). 100-kW-class radiators first fly in 2027 (struct-highflux-radiator-flight).
add_nodes.pathway: P7 (demand coupling from AI capability, not an AI-math effect)
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous demand: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
add_nodes.why: Full chain (S2): both Starship stages reflown 2027 -> 100-kW-class radiators flown on the first compute satellites 2027 -> commercial accelerators running in orbit with paying customers 2028 -> internal launch cost under ~$300/kg, Mach33's orbital-compute base-case input, 2029 -> 10 or more compute flights in one year, 2030. At about 2.1 t per AI1-class satellite, 10 flights of 100 t carry roughly 450 satellites, about 70-110 MW. This is where the AI curve meets the launch clock: frontier training compute grows ~5x a year and a GW-scale ground site takes ~2.1 years (Epoch), so S2 and S3 raise demand for compute that needs no grid interconnection. S3 is a year earlier because demand and the physical multiplier both rise from 2028; S1 is later because a capability plateau slows the build-out. More flights also speed Starship production learning. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here).
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: The economics are unproven and Mach33 itself treats space datacenters as the largest uncertainty in launch revenue; running chips near 95 C shortens their life (Mach33 reconstruction); Starlink V3 competes for the same flights through 2028; and ten compute flights in a year is a SpaceX demand decision it can defer.
add_nodes.signpost: First AI1 launch and on-orbit operation; SpaceX disclosure of a compute-satellite production rate; Starship flights carrying compute satellites in 2029 (5 or more keeps S2 on track).
add_nodes.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): New node from the advocate (proposed as physclock-compute-manifest-anchor; renamed to the trunk's domain prefix). Years moved one year later than proposed (S1 2031 / S2 2030 / S3 2029) to follow physclock-cheap-mass-internal (now 2029) and the launch-slip calibration; S3 High -> Medium (economics unproven). Labelled as an AI-capability demand effect, not AI math. Not a duplicate: struct-gw-orbital-compute is the 1 GW cumulative outcome downstream.

patch.thesis: If AI's research-grade math reaches outside engineers (2027 in the base case) and its proofs can be checked cheaply, then on-demand analysis spreads through space engineering by 2028, but new programs get schedules only about a quarter to a third shorter (an Amdahl ceiling of ~38%, a 1.6x speedup, in the base case), not 10x, because tests, factories and launches run on their own physical clock, which AI touches mainly through anomaly analysis and through demand for orbital compute rather than through mathematics.
patch.reader_hook: A research-grade result costs about $200-2,000 in tokens (the low figure counts only published successes), so 1,000 hard problems a year cost one to ten engineers before checking, and checking, not generation, sets the price; yet with only about a third of a program's critical path cognitive, Amdahl's law caps base-case schedule compression at about 38%, and realized gains are likelier 20-30%, not 10x.
patch.revision_note: B-trunk resolver (2026-10-07): Thesis: 'about a third faster' -> 'about a quarter to a third shorter' (auditor: the model computes a shorter schedule, not 1.33x faster; skeptic: 38% is a ceiling); demand coupling added.
